question: What does a patient's drug history cover?

options.A: Prescriptions, OTC items, herbs, and supplements
options.B: Surgical history and previous hospital admissions
options.C: Only traditional and cultural remedies used at home
options.D: Only prescription drugs prescribed by a doctor

explanation: A complete drug history covers every substance a patient takes, including hospital drugs, chemist items, herbs, and local supplements. You've got this! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is taking a good drug history a key safety check for nurses?

options.A: It replaces the need to check vital signs upon admission
options.B: It prevents dangerous drug interactions and reactions
options.C: It guarantees the patient will recover faster from their illness
options.D: It proves the patient is following their doctor's exact orders

explanation: Knowing all current substances helps you spot potential clashes before new treatments are given. Great nursing care starts right here! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h1)

question: When is medication reconciliation most critical for a patient?

options.B: Only when the patient is discharged home
options.C: During transitions of care between settings
options.D: Right before a surgical incision is closed

explanation: Medication reconciliation is vital whenever a patient moves between different healthcare settings or levels of care, as this is when errors happen most. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: What is the main goal of performing medication reconciliation?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of hospital pharmacy supplies
options.B: To test the memory of newly graduated nursing students
options.C: To avoid errors like missed doses, double dosing, and clashes
options.D: To force patients to buy their medications from the hospital

explanation: The core purpose is to catch and stop mistakes early, keeping your patient safe from harmful drug clashes. You're building solid clinical instincts! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which of these is NOT part of an active drug history?

options.A: Past allergies or reactions to the substance
options.B: The dose and how often the drug is taken
options.D: The exact brand or generic name of the drug

explanation: Immunizations are part of the general medical history, not an active daily drug history. Every question you answer makes clinical practice clearer! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: A patient says they take a blood pressure pill every morning. What crucial detail is still missing?

options.A: The name of the pharmacy that sold it
options.B: The color of the box the pills come in
options.C: The exact dosage strength of the pill
options.D: The weather on the day they started it

explanation: Knowing the drug name is good, but without the specific dose, you cannot assess safety or give correct care. You are thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h3)

question: Why are open-ended questions best when taking a drug history?

options.A: They are much faster to document in the nursing notes
options.B: They stop the patient from talking too much
options.C: They encourage the patient to share detailed, honest information
options.D: They prevent the patient from asking about their hospital bill

explanation: Open-ended questions let patients explain their routines in their own words instead of just saying yes or no. Excellent interviewing tip for the wards! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: What should you do if a patient cannot remember the names of their home medications?

options.A: Disregard home drugs and start fresh hospital drugs
options.B: Guess the medications based on their visible disease symptoms
options.C: Scold the patient for being careless with their health
options.D: Ask the patient or family to bring all medicine containers to the clinic

explanation: Having them bring their actual bottles or sachets gives you exact, reliable data when memory fails. Simple and practical! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h4)

question: Why do patients often forget to mention herbs and local remedies during a drug history?

options.A: These substances dissolve completely in the body within minutes
options.B: Doctors automatically know every herb sold in local markets
options.C: They view them as food or lifestyle items, not real drugs
options.D: Federal law prohibits patients from discussing herbs in hospitals

explanation: Patients view everyday teas and herbal mixtures as harmless, so they don't think to mention them. Asking probing questions bridges this gap! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: What is a major risk when patients mix herbal remedies with prescription drugs?

options.A: Unpredictable interactions can cause severe bleeding or organ damage
options.B: Herbs neutralize all chemical side effects of modern medicine
options.C: Herbal remedies always cure diseases faster than prescriptions
options.D: Prescription drugs become completely odorless inside the body

explanation: Active compounds in herbs can clash with prescriptions, leading to dangerous complications. Always screen for local remedies! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h5)

question: What does medication adherence mean in nursing care?

options.A: How strictly a pharmacist follows doctor's prescription orders
options.B: How closely a patient follows their prescribed drug routine
options.C: The speed at which a drug dissolves in the stomach
options.D: The ability of a nurse to inject medications painlessly

explanation: Adherence checks whether the patient takes their drugs correctly regarding dose, time, and frequency. You're mastering core nursing terminology! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h6)

question: What is the main danger of vague documentation in a patient's drug history?

options.A: It invites dangerous medication errors by the healthcare team
options.B: It prevents the hospital from charging appropriate patient fees
options.C: It slows down the discharge printing process by several hours
options.D: It makes the nursing notes look untidy and unprofessional

explanation: Unclear drug notes leave doctors and nurses guessing, which easily leads to wrong doses. Clear charting saves lives! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h7)

question: During a shift handover, which drug history detail is most critical to share?

options.A: The decorative color of the pill organizer brought from home
options.B: The brand name of the multivitamin taken once last year
options.C: Active high-risk medications like blood thinners and recent changes
options.D: The specific name of the retail pharmacy where drugs are bought

explanation: High-risk drugs require immediate team awareness during handovers to prevent severe adverse events. Excellent clinical judgment! [learn more](GNS215_U2_T2#GNS215_U2_T2_h7)
